name: agricultural_science_set3_p1
label: Agricultural Science: set 3 (weeds, pests and diseases, crop improvement, processing and storage, forestry)

papers.title: Weed Control: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on weed control, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Witchweed (*Striga*) is especially harmful to cereals such as maize and sorghum because it
questions.explanation:
Parasitic weeds can cause heavy losses even when few are visible, because much of the damage happens underground before the weed emerges.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- climbs over them and shades out their leaves: *Striga* is a root parasite; it does not climb over the crop.
- releases poison gas into the soil: *Striga* harms the crop by feeding on it, not with gas.
- is eaten by the pests that attack cereals: *Striga* is not a food plant for cereal pests; its harm is as a parasite.

options.label: A
options.content: attaches to their roots and takes their food and water

options.label: B
options.content: climbs over them and shades out their leaves

options.label: C
options.content: releases poison gas into the soil

options.label: D
options.content: is eaten by the pests that attack cereals

questions.stem: Spear grass (*Imperata cylindrica*) is difficult to control mainly because it
questions.explanation:
Slashing or hoeing removes only the top; the rhizomes sprout again. A systemic herbicide such as glyphosate, which moves down to the rhizomes, is effective.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is an annual that produces seeds only once: An annual completes its life in one season; spear grass lives for many years.
- is a parasite on the roots of crops: Spear grass is free-living; *Striga* is the parasitic weed.
- grows only in water: Spear grass grows on dry land; water hyacinth and water lettuce are aquatic weeds.

options.label: A
options.content: is an annual that produces seeds only once

options.label: B
options.content: is a parasite on the roots of crops

options.label: C
options.content: is a perennial that regrows from underground rhizomes

questions.stem: Nutgrass (*Cyperus*), with its triangular stem, is classified as
questions.explanation:
Grouping weeds by leaf type (grasses, broad-leaved weeds, sedges) matters because many herbicides act on one group but not the others.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a grass: Grasses have round, hollow stems and narrow leaves.
- a broad-leaved weed: Broad-leaved weeds such as *Chromolaena* have wide leaves with net veins.
- a parasitic weed: Nutgrass is free-living, not parasitic.

questions.stem: A herbicide that kills certain weeds without harming the crop, such as 2,4-D used on broad-leaved weeds in rice, is described as
questions.explanation:
Rice and maize are grasses, so 2,4-D, which acts on broad-leaved plants, kills the broad-leaved weeds and spares the crop.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- non-selective: A non-selective herbicide, such as glyphosate or paraquat, kills all green plants it touches.
- contact: A contact herbicide kills only the parts it touches; it may or may not be selective.
- pre-emergence: Pre-emergence describes the timing, before crops and weeds appear, not which plants are killed.

questions.stem: A herbicide that is absorbed by the leaves and moved through the plant to kill the roots and rhizomes is
questions.explanation:
Glyphosate is systemic, which is why it can kill perennial weeds such as spear grass.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- contact: A contact herbicide kills only the parts it touches, so rhizomes survive and regrow.
- pre-emergence: Pre-emergence herbicides are applied to the soil before weeds come up.
- selective: Selective describes which plants are killed, not how the chemical moves.

questions.stem: Which is a cultural method of weed control?
questions.explanation:
Cultural methods use good farming practice: correct spacing, cover crops, mulching, rotation, timely planting and, in swamp rice, flooding.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Spraying a herbicide: Using herbicides is chemical control.
- Pulling weeds out by hand: Hand pulling is mechanical (physical) control.
- Cleaning tools before moving to a new field: This is preventive control: it stops weed seeds being carried to new land.

options.label: C
options.content: Planting at the correct spacing so the crop canopy closes quickly and shades the weeds

options.label: D
options.content: Cleaning tools before moving to a new field

questions.stem: In swamp rice, flooding the field after transplanting helps to control weeds because
questions.explanation:
Rice tolerates standing water, but most weeds cannot germinate or grow in it, so good water control in a developed swamp reduces weeding.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the water carries herbicide to the weeds: Flooding itself is the control; no herbicide is needed for it to work.
- rice cannot grow without weeds: Weeds compete with rice; they do not help it.
- weeds are a source of food for the rice: Weeds take food from the rice; they do not supply it.

options.label: A
options.content: the water carries herbicide to the weeds

options.label: C
options.content: weeds are a source of food for the rice

options.label: D
options.content: the water drowns many weeds and stops their seeds germinating

questions.stem: Burning is NOT recommended as a method of weed control on farmland because it
questions.explanation:
Burning also kills useful soil organisms and can spread out of control into forests and other farms.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- makes the weeds grow faster afterwards: This is not the main reason; the harm is to the soil.
- adds too much nitrogen to the soil: Burning loses nitrogen as gas; it does not add it.
- is too slow to clear the land: Burning is quick; the problem is the damage it does.

options.label: A
options.content: destroys organic matter and leaves the soil bare to erosion

options.label: B
options.content: makes the weeds grow faster afterwards

options.label: C
options.content: adds too much nitrogen to the soil

options.label: D
options.content: is too slow to clear the land

papers.title: Pests and Diseases of Crops: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on pests and diseases of crops, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Swollen galls on the roots of a stunted, wilting tomato plant are a sign of attack by
questions.explanation:
Nematodes are tiny worms in the soil. Rotation with non-host crops, resistant varieties and organic matter help to control them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- stem borers: Stem borers tunnel inside stems, causing dead hearts and broken stems.
- aphids: Aphids suck sap from leaves and shoots, causing curling and spreading viruses.
- weaver birds: Weaver birds eat grain from cereal panicles.

questions.stem: A farmer sprays an insecticide on a crop suffering from a fungal leaf disease. The spray will
questions.explanation:
Identify the cause before treating: insecticides for insects, fungicides for fungi, and for virus diseases, control the vector and remove infected plants.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cure the disease, because all pesticides kill all pests: Each pesticide acts on its own target: insecticides on insects, fungicides on fungi.
- cure the disease, because fungi are insects: Fungi are not insects; they are a separate kingdom.
- make the plant resistant to the fungus: A spray does not change the plant's resistance.

options.label: A
options.content: cure the disease, because all pesticides kill all pests

options.label: B
options.content: cure the disease, because fungi are insects

options.label: C
options.content: have no effect on the disease, because insecticides do not kill fungi

options.label: D
options.content: make the plant resistant to the fungus

questions.stem: Which pest damages crops by piercing them and sucking their sap?
questions.explanation:
Piercing and sucking pests include aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs, mirids, cotton stainers and rice bugs. Many of them also spread viruses.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Grasshopper: Grasshoppers have biting and chewing mouthparts.
- Fall armyworm: Fall armyworm caterpillars bite and chew leaves.
- Termite: Termites chew roots, stems and wood.

questions.stem: Laws that stop infected plants and seeds from entering the country are an example of
questions.explanation:
Quarantine keeps new pests and diseases out; once a pest is established, it is very hard to remove.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cultural control: Cultural control uses farming practices such as rotation and sanitation.
- biological control: Biological control uses natural enemies of the pest.
- chemical control: Chemical control uses pesticides.

questions.stem: In integrated pest management (IPM), pesticides are used
questions.explanation:
IPM combines resistant varieties, cultural practices, natural enemies and careful monitoring, so chemicals are used as little as possible.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- on a fixed schedule every week, whatever the pest numbers: Spraying by the calendar wastes money and kills natural enemies.
- never, under any circumstances: IPM allows pesticides as a last step, used correctly and only when needed.
- instead of all other methods: IPM combines several methods; chemicals are only one of them.

options.label: A
options.content: on a fixed schedule every week, whatever the pest numbers

options.label: B
options.content: only when pest numbers reach the level that would cause economic loss

questions.stem: Which pesticide formulation is a liquid that is mixed with water to form an emulsion for spraying?
questions.explanation:
The formulation code is printed on the label. Always read the label for the rate, the protective clothing needed and the waiting period before harvest.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Wettable powder (WP): A wettable powder is a powder mixed with water, not a liquid.
- Granules: Granules are coarse grains applied to the soil or into the whorl, not mixed for spraying.
- Dust: A dust is a fine powder applied dry.

questions.stem: Fumigation of large grain stores should be carried out only by trained, licensed people because
questions.explanation:
Fumigants penetrate stored produce to kill insects inside the grain, but they can kill anyone who breathes them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- fumigants work only when applied by government officers: The chemistry is the same whoever applies it; the danger is why training is needed.
- fumigation makes the grain germinate: Fumigation does not make grain germinate.
- fumigants are expensive fertilisers: Fumigants are pesticides, not fertilisers.

options.label: A
options.content: fumigants work only when applied by government officers

options.label: D
options.content: fumigants are gases that are deadly to people as well as pests

questions.stem: Seedlings in a nursery bed suddenly collapse at soil level and die. This disease is called
questions.explanation:
Damping off is caused by soil fungi in wet, crowded conditions. Good drainage, sowing thinly and not overwatering help prevent it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mosaic: Mosaic is a mottled yellow and green pattern on leaves, caused by viruses.
- leaf spot: Leaf spot is a disease that causes spots on the leaves.
- dieback: Dieback is the death of branches from the tips backwards, as caused by mirids on cocoa.

papers.title: Crop Improvement and Breeding: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on crop improvement and breeding, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In pure-line selection,
questions.explanation:
Pure-line selection suits self-pollinated crops such as rice and cowpea, and gives a uniform new variety.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- seed from many good plants is mixed together and sown: Mixing seed from many good plants is mass selection.
- two different varieties are crossed to combine their qualities: Crossing two varieties is hybridisation.
- seeds are treated with radiation to cause new traits: Treating seeds with radiation is mutation breeding.

options.label: A
options.content: seed from many good plants is mixed together and sown

options.label: B
options.content: the seed of single outstanding plants of a self-pollinated crop is grown separately and the best line is chosen

options.label: C
options.content: two different varieties are crossed to combine their qualities

options.label: D
options.content: seeds are treated with radiation to cause new traits

questions.stem: The extra vigour and yield shown by the first generation (F₁) from crossing two unrelated parents is called
questions.explanation:
Hybrid maize uses hybrid vigour to give high yields.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- polyploidy: Polyploidy is having extra sets of chromosomes.
- mutation: A mutation is a change in a gene or chromosome.
- dormancy: Dormancy is a resting period of a seed.

questions.stem: A farmer saves seed from a field of hybrid maize and plants it the next season. The farmer is most likely to get
questions.explanation:
Hybrid seed must be bought new each season. Seed of open-pollinated varieties can be saved and replanted.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a crop exactly like the hybrid, with the same high yield: Hybrid vigour is lost in the next generation, because the offspring segregate.
- a crop with even more hybrid vigour: Vigour falls, not rises, when hybrid seed is replanted.
- seed that will not germinate at all: The seed usually germinates; the problem is a weaker, uneven crop.

options.label: A
options.content: a crop exactly like the hybrid, with the same high yield

options.label: B
options.content: a crop with even more hybrid vigour

options.label: C
options.content: seed that will not germinate at all

options.label: D
options.content: a mixed, weaker crop with a lower yield

questions.stem: Crossing the offspring of a cross back to one of its parents, in order to transfer one useful gene such as disease resistance into a good variety, is called
questions.explanation:
Repeated backcrossing keeps nearly all the good variety's qualities while adding the one desired gene.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mass selection: Mass selection chooses many good plants from a crop and bulks their seed.
- introduction: Introduction is bringing in a variety from another place and testing it.
- tissue culture: Tissue culture grows many identical plantlets from small pieces of tissue.

questions.stem: Certified seed is preferred to seed saved from a farmer's own crop because certified seed
questions.explanation:
Seed classes run breeder seed → foundation seed → certified seed. Certified seed is grown by approved growers, inspected in the field and labelled.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- never needs fertiliser to give a good yield: Even the best seed needs good soil and nutrients.
- is always cheaper than saved seed: Certified seed usually costs more; it is worth the price because of its quality.
- can be saved and replanted for ever without any loss: Seed saved year after year slowly becomes mixed and diseased.

options.label: A
options.content: never needs fertiliser to give a good yield

options.label: B
options.content: is tested for purity, germination and freedom from disease

options.label: C
options.content: is always cheaper than saved seed

options.label: D
options.content: can be saved and replanted for ever without any loss

questions.stem: Orange-fleshed sweet potato and yellow cassava have been bred mainly to
questions.explanation:
Breeding for better nutrition is one aim of crop improvement, alongside yield, resistance, tolerance, early maturity and quality.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- resist drought completely: Their main aim is better nutrition; drought tolerance is a separate breeding aim.
- produce more starch for industry: Their orange or yellow colour comes from vitamin A precursors, not extra starch.
- mature in two weeks: No root crop matures in two weeks.

options.label: C
options.content: provide more vitamin A in the diet

questions.stem: NERICA rice was developed by crossing *Oryza glaberrima* with *Oryza sativa*. From the African parent it gained
questions.explanation:
Breeders combined the hardiness of African rice with the yield of Asian rice, then selected among the offspring.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its very high yield: High yield came mainly from the Asian parent, *Oryza sativa*.
- resistance to every rice disease: No variety resists every disease.
- the ability to grow without any water: All rice needs water; NERICA tolerates drought better, but still needs water.

options.label: C
options.content: the ability to grow without any water

options.label: D
options.content: tolerance of weeds, drought and poor soils

questions.stem: Which institution in Sierra Leone carries out teaching and research in agriculture?
questions.explanation:
Njala and the agricultural research institutes test new varieties, such as cassava resistant to mosaic disease, before they are released to farmers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Fourah Bay College: Fourah Bay College is known mainly for arts, sciences and engineering, not agricultural research.
- Bank of Sierra Leone: The Bank of Sierra Leone is the central bank.
- National Revenue Authority: The National Revenue Authority collects taxes.

papers.title: Crop Processing and Storage: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on crop processing and storage, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A farmer harvests 600 kg of maize grain with a moisture content of 25% and dries it to 10%. What will the grain weigh after drying?
questions.explanation:
Dry matter = 75% of 600 kg = 450 kg. After drying, the dry matter is 90% of the new mass, so new mass = 450 ÷ 0.90 = 500 kg.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 450 kg: 450 kg is the dry matter alone; the dried grain still contains 10% water.
- 510 kg: This takes 15% (25% − 10%) off the fresh mass, but the percentages are of different totals.
- 540 kg: This takes only 10% off the fresh mass.

questions.stem: Groundnuts stored while still damp may develop moulds that produce aflatoxins. Aflatoxins are dangerous because they
questions.explanation:
Proper drying, sorting out mouldy nuts and dry storage prevent aflatoxin contamination.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- make the groundnuts germinate in store: Aflatoxins are poisons; sprouting is a separate effect of damp storage.
- attract weevils into the store: Aflatoxins are not insect attractants.
- add extra protein to the groundnuts: Aflatoxins are poisons, not nutrients.

options.label: A
options.content: make the groundnuts germinate in store

options.label: B
options.content: are poisons that can damage the liver of people and animals who eat them

options.label: D
options.content: add extra protein to the groundnuts

questions.stem: A crib, a narrow slatted structure raised on legs with rat guards, is used to store
questions.explanation:
Air flows through the slats and dries the cobs further; the raised legs and rat guards keep out rodents.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- yam tubers: Yams are stored in an airy, shaded barn, tied to frames or racks.
- fresh fish: Fresh fish needs a cold store or must be smoked or dried.
- palm oil: Palm oil is stored in clean, closed containers.

questions.stem: Grain stored in hermetic (airtight) bags is protected from insects because
questions.explanation:
Insects already in the grain use up the oxygen and die, and no new ones can get in. The grain must be dry when it is sealed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the bags contain a strong insecticide: Hermetic bags work without chemicals.
- insects cannot see grain through the plastic: The protection comes from lack of oxygen, not from hiding the grain.
- the grain inside keeps germinating: Grain in airtight bags does not germinate; it stays dormant.

options.label: A
options.content: the bags contain a strong insecticide

options.label: B
options.content: insects cannot see grain through the plastic

options.label: D
options.content: the insects die from lack of oxygen, without any chemicals

questions.stem: Rice panicles and seed maize are often kept on a loft above the kitchen fire because
questions.explanation:
The kitchen loft is a traditional storage method that uses the household's own fire to protect grain and seed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the fire cooks the grain so it keeps longer: The grain is kept above the fire, not cooked by it.
- rats prefer to stay near fires: Rats are not attracted to a smoky loft; the smoke and heat help protect the produce.
- the heat makes the seeds germinate faster: The aim is to keep seeds dry and dormant until planting.

options.label: A
options.content: smoke and heat keep the produce dry and repel insects

options.label: B
options.content: the fire cooks the grain so it keeps longer

options.label: C
options.content: rats prefer to stay near fires

options.label: D
options.content: the heat makes the seeds germinate faster

questions.stem: Which practice helps to prevent pest attack in a grain store?
questions.explanation:
Dry the produce well, clean and repair the store, sort out damaged grain, raise bags on pallets and keep rats out.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Mixing the new harvest with old grain left in the store: Insects in old grain spread quickly into the new harvest.
- Stacking bags directly on a damp floor against the walls: Bags on a damp floor absorb moisture and go mouldy; they should be on pallets, away from walls.
- Storing the grain before it is fully dry: Damp grain goes mouldy and encourages insects.

options.label: A
options.content: Mixing the new harvest with old grain left in the store

options.label: B
options.content: Cleaning out the store completely before filling it with the new harvest

options.label: C
options.content: Stacking bags directly on a damp floor against the walls

options.label: D
options.content: Storing the grain before it is fully dry

questions.stem: In processing oil palm fruit, the bunches are first sterilised (boiled or steamed). Which is a reason for this?
questions.explanation:
Oil palm processing: sterilise, thresh, digest, press, clarify; the nuts are cracked for kernels and kernel oil.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It removes the kernels from the nuts: Kernels are removed later by cracking the nuts.
- It turns the oil into palm wine: Palm wine is tapped from the living palm, not made from the fruit.
- It makes the fruit ferment to add flavour: Fermenting is part of cocoa processing; sterilising palm fruit stops spoilage.

options.label: A
options.content: It removes the kernels from the nuts

options.label: B
options.content: It turns the oil into palm wine

options.label: C
options.content: It stops the enzymes that make the oil go rancid, and loosens the fruit from the bunch

options.label: D
options.content: It makes the fruit ferment to add flavour

questions.stem: Processing crops such as cassava into gari is important to farmers mainly because it
questions.explanation:
Fresh cassava roots spoil within two or three days of harvest; gari keeps for months and sells for more.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increases the weight of the produce: Processing usually reduces weight, as water is removed.
- makes the produce perish more quickly: Processing makes produce keep longer, not shorter.
- is needed before any crop can be eaten: Many crops are eaten fresh; processing is done to store, transport and add value.

options.label: A
options.content: increases the weight of the produce

options.label: B
options.content: makes the produce perish more quickly

options.label: C
options.content: is needed before any crop can be eaten

options.label: D
options.content: makes the produce safe to store for longer, adds value and removes poisons

papers.title: Forestry and Agroforestry: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on forestry and agroforestry, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the taungya system,
questions.explanation:
Taungya gives farmers land for food crops and gives the forest department free weeding until the tree canopy closes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- food crops are grown in alleys between rows of pruned leguminous trees: This is alley cropping.
- animals graze under trees that give them shade and fodder: This is silvopasture.
- rows of trees are planted to protect crops from wind: These are windbreaks or shelterbelts.

options.label: A
options.content: farmers grow food crops between young timber trees in a new plantation, weeding the trees as they weed their crops

options.label: B
options.content: food crops are grown in alleys between rows of pruned leguminous trees

options.label: C
options.content: animals graze under trees that give them shade and fodder

options.label: D
options.content: rows of trees are planted to protect crops from wind

questions.stem: In alley cropping, trees such as *Gliricidia* and *Leucaena* are planted in rows mainly because they
questions.explanation:
The prunings are used as mulch and green manure, improving fertility without costly fertiliser.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- produce the most valuable timber: They are chosen for soil improvement, not timber.
- shade out the food crops in the alleys: The trees are pruned so they do not shade the crops.
- attract pests away from the crops: This is not why they are planted.

options.label: B
options.content: are legumes whose prunings add nitrogen and organic matter to the soil

options.label: C
options.content: shade out the food crops in the alleys

options.label: D
options.content: attract pests away from the crops

questions.stem: Planting trees on land where there was no forest before is called
questions.explanation:
Afforestation and reforestation are both artificial regeneration, because trees are planted.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- reforestation: Reforestation is replanting where a forest has been cut down.
- natural regeneration: Natural regeneration is letting a forest regrow on its own from seeds, stumps and roots.
- deforestation: Deforestation is the clearing of forest.

questions.stem: Which is the main cause of the high demand on Sierra Leone's forests for wood?
questions.explanation:
Charcoal and firewood are cheap and widely used, so cutting for fuel is a major cause of deforestation around towns.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Paper made from local trees: Little paper is made from local trees.
- Wooden ships built for export: Shipbuilding is not a major use of the forests.
- Railway sleepers: Sierra Leone's railway closed decades ago.

options.label: D
options.content: Firewood and charcoal, the main cooking fuels for most households

questions.stem: Which of the following is an effect of deforestation?
questions.explanation:
Forests protect catchments, hold soil, store carbon and shelter wildlife; clearing them reverses all of these.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- More rainfall soaking slowly into the soil: Without trees, rain runs off quickly instead of soaking in.
- More habitat for chimpanzees and forest elephants: Clearing forest destroys their habitat.
- Less carbon dioxide in the air: Cutting and burning forests releases carbon dioxide.

options.label: A
options.content: More soil erosion, flooding and drying of streams

options.label: B
options.content: More rainfall soaking slowly into the soil

options.label: C
options.content: More habitat for chimpanzees and forest elephants

options.label: D
options.content: Less carbon dioxide in the air

questions.stem: Young trees in a forest plantation must be protected with firebreaks during the dry season because
questions.explanation:
A plantation also needs weeding, thinning and pruning for several years; it is not finished once it is planted.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- firebreaks supply water to the trees: A firebreak is a cleared strip of land; it does not supply water.
- young trees need regular burning to grow: Fire kills young trees.
- firebreaks are used to harvest the timber: Firebreaks are for protection, not harvesting.

options.label: A
options.content: firebreaks supply water to the trees

options.label: B
options.content: a single bush fire can destroy the whole plantation

options.label: C
options.content: young trees need regular burning to grow

options.label: D
options.content: firebreaks are used to harvest the timber

questions.stem: Growing cocoa or coffee under taller shade trees, with plantain between them, is an example of
questions.explanation:
Each layer uses light at a different height, and the trees protect the soil and provide shade the cocoa needs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- monocropping: Monocropping is growing a single crop on its own.
- shifting cultivation: Shifting cultivation moves the farm and homestead to new land.
- pastoral farming: Pastoral farming is herding animals.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-timber forest product?
questions.explanation:
Non-timber forest products include honey, fruits, nuts, mushrooms, snails, medicines, rattan, bamboo, raffia and kola.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sawn planks: Planks are timber.
- Electricity poles: Poles are timber products.
- Logs for export: Logs are timber.
